description: The most relevant reasons why populism causes costs, each linked to populism with 'can cause' and quantified by the studies that report it for the average populist episode and per country: the loss of GDP per capita and of consumption (Funke, Schularick & Trebesch 2023), the rise of the public debt and the drop of the financial integration (Funke et al.), the economic nationalism with the US tariffs of 2018 (Fajgelbaum et al. 2020) and the Brexit (Born et al. 2019, CER 2022, OBR), the institutional erosion with the democratic backsliding (Kyle & Mounk 2018) and the EU funds lost by Hungary under the rule of law conditionality, and the excess mortality of the COVID-19 pandemic (Bayerlein et al. 2021). The annual GDP decline of populism and its solution are stated in problem_populism.json instead, because they are the row of the global problem ranking of the start page. Venezuela under Chávez and Maduro, a populist episode of Funke et al., is added as the extreme case of the collapse of GDP, the hyperinflation and the emigration; these values are not attributed to populism by their sources, because the fall of the oil price and the sanctions are also causes, so they do not carry a '<reason> due to populism' triple. Every number is taken from the named source as reported; a country that a study does not report is left out and never estimated. A share is stored as the decimal ratio, a loss as a positive number and a change with its sign. Each study has its own sample and metric, so numbers of different studies are not comparable without reading the source description. Every amount of money is stated in euro: the US dollar figure of the source is converted with the ECB 2023 annual average of 1.0813 USD per EUR (the value of GDP.json) whatever the price base year of the source, and the source figure is kept in the description of the value. A value of a reason carries the triple '<reason> due to populism' and not the word 'populism' itself, because a value that names a global problem directly is a row of the global problem ranking of the start page, where only the potential loss and the solution of a problem belong.

sources.name: Fajgelbaum et al. (2020)
sources.description: Fajgelbaum, P. D., Goldberg, P. K., Kennedy, P. J., Khandelwal, A. K. (2020): The Return to Protectionism. Quarterly Journal of Economics 135(1), 1-55. Abstract: the US import tariffs of 2018 were fully passed through to the duty-inclusive prices; the loss of the US buyers of imports is USD 51 billion or 0.27 percent of the GDP; after the tariff revenue and the gains of the domestic producers the aggregate real income loss is USD 7.2 billion or 0.04 percent of the GDP. Trump (2017-) is a populist leader in the list of Funke et al.

sources.name: Born et al. (2019)
sources.description: Born, B., Müller, G. J., Schularick, M., Sedláček, P. (2019): The Costs of Economic Nationalism: Evidence from the Brexit Experiment. The Economic Journal 129(623), 2722-2744. Abstract: by the end of 2018 the Brexit vote has caused an output loss of 1.7 to 2.5 percent of the GDP compared to a synthetic control without the vote, mainly by a downward revision of the growth expectations.

sources.name: Springford (2022) CER cost of Brexit
sources.description: Springford, J. (2022): Centre for European Reform, doppelgänger estimate of December 2022: the GDP of the United Kingdom was 5.5 percent lower in the second quarter of 2022 than in a synthetic United Kingdom that stayed in the European Union, i.e. GBP 33 billion in that quarter and about GBP 40 billion of tax revenue per year; there is an estimation error around the number.

sources.name: OBR Brexit analysis
sources.description: Office for Budget Responsibility: the long run assumption of its forecasts, unchanged up to the Spring Budget 2025, that the Brexit lowers the imports and exports of the United Kingdom by 15 percent and the potential productivity by 4 percent compared to a remaining in the European Union, with the full impact after about 15 years; an assumption based on the average of external studies, not a measured loss.

sources.name: Kyle & Mounk (2018) The Populist Harm to Democracy
sources.description: Kyle, J., Mounk, Y. (2018): The Populist Harm to Democracy: An Empirical Assessment. Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. 46 populist leaders in democracies 1990-2018: 23 percent of the populists cause a significant democratic backsliding compared with 6 percent of the non-populist democratically elected leaders; only 34 percent of the populist leaders leave office after a free and fair election or because they respect the term limits.

sources.name: Bayerlein et al. (2021)
sources.description: Bayerlein, M., Boese, V. A., Gates, S., Kamin, K., Murshed, S. M. (2021): Populism and COVID-19: How Populist Governments (Mis)Handle the Pandemic. Journal of Political Institutions and Political Economy 2(3), 389-428. 42 countries with weekly data of 2020: the excess mortality of the countries with a populist government exceeds the one of the non-populist countries by 8 percentage points (i.e. 98 percent); a cross-country correlation; the Kiel working paper of July 2021 stated 10 percentage points.

sources.name: EU rule of law conditionality Hungary
sources.description: Council Implementing Decision of 15 December 2022 under the conditionality regulation (EU) 2020/2092: about EUR 6.3 billion of the cohesion funds of Hungary were frozen because of the corruption, the conflicts of interest and the public procurement; the first tranche of EUR 1.04 billion expired at the end of 2024 without the reforms and is lost for Hungary, as stated by the European Commission; Orbán (2010-) is a populist leader in the list of Funke et al.

sources.name: ECLAC (2020) Preliminary Overview Venezuela
sources.description: Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (2020): Preliminary Overview of the Economies of Latin America and the Caribbean, country note Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela: the economic activity fell by 30 percent in 2020, the seventh year in a row, a cumulative drop of 74 percent since 2013; a preliminary estimate.

sources.name: ECLAC Venezuela inflation 2018
sources.description: Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, country note Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela: inflation of 130'060.2 percent in 2018 according to the Banco Central de Venezuela, after hyperinflation had taken hold in November 2017; the IMF estimated about 1'370'000 percent.

sources.name: R4V (2024) Refugees and migrants from Venezuela
sources.description: Inter-Agency Coordination Platform for Refugees and Migrants from Venezuela (R4V), co-led by UNHCR and IOM: 7.77 million refugees and migrants from Venezuela worldwide in May 2024, 6.59 million of them in Latin America and the Caribbean.
